1.pericope_label: The rose of Sharon, the lily among thorns, and the apple tree among the trees of the wood

schools.summary: Identify the plants before interpreting them, weighing narcissus, crocus, mallow and meadow-saffron for the flower and quince, citron, apple and apricot for the tree against explicit requirements of shade, taste, perfume and colour, and reading the grammar so that she claims to be one of a class and not the one.
Take the modest self-description as the church's and the answering comparisons as Christ's, and run the preference up through the ranks of angels and princes to set the beloved above them all.
Give the opening words to the bridegroom or read them as a bride's modesty answering a compliment, and keep the identification of the tree no further than apple or citron.
Hear condescension in the comparison, the Son of the Highest owning himself a common flower, and divide the tree's benefit into the shade that shelters and the fruit that feeds.

debates.question: Who says I am the rose of Sharon?

positions.view: the bridegroom, comparing himself to rose and lily for fragrance and beauty
the bride, in modesty answering a compliment by calling herself a common flower of the field
uncertain, though most Jewish writers take it of the church and that reading bids fair
the sweet-scented narcissus, the derivation pointing to a bulb and no bulb being more fragrant, though the crocus and the mallow have been proposed
the meadow saffron of the Syriac, the flesh-coloured flower on a leafless stem called son before father because the blossom precedes the leaves
a rose, and best rendered a rose of the field with almost all the versions

outliers.reading: Alone settles the tree by explicit criteria and elimination, requiring grateful shade, agreeable taste, sweet perfume and a golden appearance, setting aside the apple because the Palestine fruit so called is really a quince and the climate is too hot, rejecting the quince on taste since it is astringent until cooked, leaving the citron disputed on shade, and awarding it to the apricot as the only candidate meeting every requirement.

themes: I am the rose of Sharon, and the lily of the valleys.
As the lily among thorns, so is my love among the daughters.
As the apple tree among the trees of the wood, so is my beloved among the sons. I sat down under his shadow with great delight, and his fruit was sweet to my taste.

4.pericope_label: The banqueting house: stay me with flagons, and my beloved like a roe on the mountains

schools.summary: Strip the scene of furniture and doctrine alike: the house of wine is the place of love's delights, the flagons a dried cake of uncertain material, the sleeper a woman and not a man, and the daughters present only in the poet's imagination.
Read the banqueting house as the gospel feast and the two hands as blessings of both kinds, while leaving open whether the church or Christ speaks the adjuration.

Furnish the passage from antiquity and from experience: wine kept in jars along an upper wall as Homer describes, a rustic form of oath, and a courtyard wall behind which the bridegroom is first seen.
Take the recognition of the voice as the mark of the sheep who knows its shepherd, and find the triumph in the claim that no other voice can speak to the heart.

debates.question: What is the house of wine?

positions.view: an upper store-room where wine stood in jars against the wall with the household's most precious things
a banqueting house, and figuratively the gospel feast in the house of God
the chamber where the king entertains his friends, not the vineyard, which would be named differently
neither cellar nor banqueting hall nor vineyard, but simply the place of the delights of love

debates.question: Who is not to be awakened, and by whom is the charge given?

positions.view: the reading is till she please, not till he, and the poet is playfully telling her companions not to intrude on his beloved's sleep
either the church or Christ may be speaking, with reasons on both sides
some rustic form of adjuration, at which the first night ends

outliers.reading: Alone catalogues what allegory has made of a single clause, listing five readings of the wall the beloved stands behind: our mortal condition; the middle wall of partition, the law; the iniquities that keep a voice from reaching us; the creatures behind whom God stands and through whom he speaks; and, on Bossuet's authority and with an apology for saying it, the flesh of Christ spread over his divinity, through which it sounds sweetly and alters its voice.

themes: He brought me to the banqueting house, and his banner over me was love.
Stay me with flagons, comfort me with apples: for I am sick of love.
His left hand is under my head, and his right hand doth embrace me.
I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please.
The voice of my beloved! behold, he cometh leaping upon the mountains, skipping upon the hills.
My beloved is like a roe or a young hart: behold, he standeth behind our wall, he looketh forth at the windows, shewing himself through the lattice.

10.pericope_label: Rise up, my love: the winter past, the little foxes, and the day breaking

schools.summary: Deny that the scene is a dream, date the season and the hour from the vocabulary, and place the fox song in a recognised poetic genre rather than in an allegory.
Read the speaking as an answer to unspoken prayer and the seasons as the states of the soul before and after conversion, and leave the order about the foxes to Christ and the church together.
Import the climate and the natural history: a named forty-day cold season at Aleppo, a fig tree never wholly bare, foxes trapped among the young clusters, and a daybreak that breathes.

Moralise the dove into the graces it stands for, beauty and innocence and quietness and a faithfulness like the turtle's to her mate, the dove that descended on Christ descending on Christians to make them meek.

debates.question: What is the winter that is past?

positions.view: a particular severe cold season with its own name, since the Hebrew word occurs nowhere else and another word covers the rainy season generally
the season of cloud and gloom, from a root meaning to overcast
the rainy season itself, from a root meaning to conceal or veil, winter in the East being simply the rains
a figure for the state of the soul before conversion, and of Jew and Gentile before Christ

debates.question: Who says Take us the foxes?

positions.view: Shulamith, singing a vine-dresser's ditty natural to a girl who had kept a vineyard
the bridegroom, instructing his companions as he enters
Christ or the church, or perhaps both together, addressing the ministers of the word
the poem itself, in the traditional manner of warning troublesome creatures away from a wedding

debates.question: What hour is until the day break?

positions.view: dawn, since the word means to breathe and first light comes with refreshing breezes
evening, the day breathing as it cools when the breeze sets in, fixed by shadows that flee by lengthening
before the evening comes, so that what is asked may be done first

outliers.reading: Alone refuses the allegorical reading of the foxes by placing the verse in a genre, comparing the warning-off addressed by poets in wedding songs to mischievous creatures, as Spenser banishes owls and ravens and frogs from a wedding night and Theocritus curses the brush-tailed foxes that spoil a neighbour's vines, and noting only in passing that in the allegorising commentators they stand for heretics.

themes: My beloved spake, and said unto me, Rise up, my love, my fair one, and come away.
For, lo, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone;
The flowers appear on the earth; the time of the singing of birds is come, and the voice of the turtle is heard in our land;
The fig tree putteth forth her green figs, and the vines with the tender grape give a good smell. Arise, my love, my fair one, and come away.
O my dove, that art in the clefts of the rock, in the secret places of the stairs, let me see thy countenance, let me hear thy voice; for sweet is thy voice, and thy countenance is comely.
Take us the foxes, the little foxes, that spoil the vines: for our vines have tender grapes.
My beloved is mine, and I am his: he feedeth among the lilies.
Until the day break, and the shadows flee away, turn, my beloved, and be thou like a roe or a young hart upon the mountains of Bether.
